dataset.name: Results of Experimental Additions of Organic Nitrogen on Soil Organic Matter Decomposition, Teller Road Site, Seward Peninsula, 2017 and 2018
description: This dataset provides the results of the experimental addition of glutamic acid on anaerobic organic matter decomposition as measured in the field and through laboratory methods. Field experiments were conducted during the summers of 2017 and 2018 at the NGEE Arctic Teller Road Site at mile marker 27 (TL_MM27) near Intensive Site 9 (TL_IS_9). At the field site, a solution of glutamate (13C- and 15N-labeled glutamate in 2017, unlabeled in 2018) was injected belowground and investigators observed the resulting changes in downslope porewater geochemistry and dissolved greenhouse gas concentrations. Soil collected near the site in 2017 was used in a laboratory column flow-through experiment with added glutamate. Results of porewater geochemistry, dissolved greenhouse gasses, and organic matter composition analyses for 2017 and 2018 experiments are provided. There are six *.csv data files and one *.pdf user guide.

The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research. The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska. Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

Site description
An experimental plot was established near mile marker 27 on the Teller Road, northwest of Nome, Alaska (N 64.758839, W 165.979295). The site is located in tussock tundra at the toe of a hillslope characterized by degraded peat plateaus with sedge-rich pools in between. Standing water was present in the inter-tussock areas, indicating the water table was at or near the soil surface. Soils were primarily organic matter in the upper 38 cm (> 25% C), transitioning to a more mineral rich soil near 56 cm depth (11% C). Surface soils (to approximately 10 cm depth) were collected from the plot at the end of the 2017 field experiment for use in the laboratory soil column experiments. The average daily temperature during the 2017 experiment was 12.4 °C and a rain event coincided with the final 18 h of the experiment (Busey et al., 2017). The mean temperature during the 2018 experiment was ∼10 °C with intermittent rain throughout.

2017 Field Experiment
The ﬁrst ﬁeld experiment was conducted August 8–12, 2017. A series of piezometers and rhizons were installed to collect soil pore water from the subsurface of the experimental plot. We used a combination of piezometers and rhizons to optimally sample pore water at diﬀerent depths. Piezometers generally ﬁlled more quickly, but sometimes did not ﬁll at all when installed near the surface. Most rhizons ﬁlled slowly but reliably at all depths, enabling porewater sampling from the shallow soil. Piezometers were installed in pairs on a 2-m linear transect downslope from the selected injection point (Fig. 2). Deep piezometers (“D”) were inserted 50 cm below the soil surface, and shallow piezometers (“T”) were 25 cm below the surface. Rhizons were installed at 35 cm depth 28 and 60 cm downslope of the injection point. Two additional rhizons were installed perpendicular to the downslope transect (60 cm downslope and 43 cm to either side) to capture possible lateral transport of the injected solution in the subsurface.
An additional piezometer was installed at the injection point and inserted 20–35 cm below the soil surface for the injection of the tracer solution into the subsurface at 20–35 cm. The injection solution was 500 mL of 2000 mg L−1 (25.0 mM) Br− (as KBr) and 800 mg L−1 (5.23 mM) of universally 13C- and 15N-labeled L-glutamic acid (Glu; 99%; Cambridge Isotope Laboratories). The solution was added to the subsurface through the piezometer at the injection point using a syringe.
Porewater samples were collected from the rhizons and piezometers 1, 6, 25, 43, 62, and 76 h after the injection. The sampling frequency and volume were limited by the rate at which the piezometers ﬁlled with porewater. Therefore, some samples from multiple rhizons and piezometers were pooled to obtain suﬃcient water volume for chemical and isotope analysis. The shallow (25 cm) piezo- meters (T1, T2, and T3) ﬁlled slowly and were only used for Fe(II) analysis.
Samples for isotope and geochemical analysis were ﬁltered through a 0.2 μm nylon membrane and collected in serum bottles precombusted at 550 °C for four hours, ﬁlled to capacity to exclude headspace.
The bottles were crimp-capped with acid washed rubber septa to avoid gas exchange. Samples were stored and transported in coolers at ∼4 °C until analysis. pH and Fe(II) concentrations were measured in the field using a Hanna Instruments portable pH meter, and using a Hach DR 900 with the colorimetric 1,10-phenanthroline method (Hach method 8146), respectively.

2018 ﬁeld experiment
A second ﬁeld experiment was conducted August 23–29, 2018 to replicate the key ﬁndings from the ﬁrst experiment. An experimental plot was established ∼20 m away from the plot used in the 2017 experiment, consisting of six rhizons. The rhizons were installed in pairs at the same depth (45 cm) 0.4, 1.4, and 2.4 m downslope of an injection piezometer (also installed at 45 cm depth). Samples from the duplicate rhizons were pooled to obtain suﬃcient porewater for all analyses. A smaller volume of injection solution with a higher concentration (150 mL of 2667 mg L−1 Glu and 5000 mg L−1 Br−) was used so that the amount of added glutamate was the same in both experiments. The glutamate used for the 2018 experiment was not isotopically labeled. Samples were collected before the injection and after 1, 3, 5, 21, 43, and 93 h. Samples were ﬁltered and analyzed for pH and Fe(II) using the same procedure as the 2017 experiment.

Lab column experiments
A glass column (2.5 × 20.3 cm) was ﬁlled with ﬁeld-moist soil collected from the study site in 2017. A mixture of surface and pore waters collected nearby was used as the eluent, to mimic the organic and in- organic chemical characteristics of the in situ subsurface environment. The eluent solution was capped and ﬂushed with N2 for one hour to remove dissolved O2. A gas bag ﬁlled with N2 was connected to the eluent bottle to maintain anoxia while preventing the pump from drawing a vacuum in the sealed bottle. Then, the anoxic solution was circulated through the soil column for 96 h at 0.12 bed volumes hour−1 for initial conditioning. The ﬂow rate was reduced to 0.08 bed volumes hour−1 prior to the start of the experiments.
Br− (as KBr) and Glu were dissolved directly in the eluent solution (concentrations of 300 and 500 mg L−1, respectively), which was ﬂushed again with N2 then pumped through the column for a continuous injection of the tracer and N. A fraction collector was programmed to collect the eﬄuent from the soil column every 35 min initially, changing to every 20 min after four hours (for better temporal resolution during breakthrough) and returning to 35 min intervals after six hours. Selected samples were analyzed for Fe(II) concentrations immediately after collection using the 1,10-phenanthroline method. Samples were analyzed within 24 h of collection or frozen until analysis.

Chemical analyses
Samples of porewater collected in the field and the eluent samples from the column experiment were analyzed for numerous chemical constituents and isotopic composition. Please refer to Philben et al. (2018) for details.
